2.1.summary:
Expect difficult people, and decide in advance how you'll meet them. People behave badly because they've misunderstood what's actually good for them, not because they're monsters. And since they share the same human nature and the same capacity to reason as you, they're kin, not enemies.

They can't really harm you, because no one else can make you act badly. Getting angry or giving them the cold shoulder goes against what we're built for: working together, like two hands.
2.1.today: Before the commute or the first meeting, take a moment to expect the person who pushes into the queue, the colleague who takes the credit, the reply-all that annoys you. Having pictured it already, you're more likely to respond calmly than to snap.

2.2.summary:
You are made of three things: a body, the breath that keeps it alive, and your mind, the part that thinks and decides. The body is just blood, bones and a tangle of nerves; the breath is air going in and out. Only the mind really matters.

Marcus is talking to himself as an ageing man. Put the books down, he says, and stop letting your mind be jerked about like a puppet by impulses, resenting the present or dreading the future.

2.3.summary:
Everything that happens is part of one ordered whole. Even what looks like chance is woven into the larger pattern, and whatever keeps the universe going is good for each part of it, including you. The universe sustains itself through constant change, as elements and the things made of them transform.

Marcus tells himself to hold on to these few principles and drop his hunger for more books, so that he can die cheerfully and gratefully instead of grumbling.

2.4.summary: Marcus is scolding himself for procrastinating. He's had chance after chance to get his thinking straight and hasn't taken them. He is part of a vast universe, his time in it is limited, and if he doesn't use that time to clear his mind, it will run out and never come back.
2.4.today: Think of the book you've meant to read for years, the conversation you keep postponing, or the habit you'll start 'after this busy patch'. There's always another busy patch, and the time doesn't wait.

2.5.summary:
Focus completely on what you're doing right now, and do it with dignity, warmth, honesty and fairness, setting other thoughts aside. The way to manage that is to treat each action as if it were your last: no carelessness, no acting on impulse against your better judgement, no pretence, no self-absorption, no resentment of your lot.

Marcus notes how little is actually required. Get these few things right and life runs calmly, and nothing more is asked of you.
2.5.today: Answering an email while half-watching a video and thinking about dinner is the opposite of this. Try giving one task your full attention, as if it were the last thing you'd do today, and notice how much better it goes.

2.6.summary: Marcus speaks harshly to his own soul. Go on, he says, keep wronging yourself; you won't have long left to make it right. A single life is enough to live well, but he's spending his by letting his happiness depend on what other people think of him.
2.6.today: Checking how many people liked your post, replaying whether the boss seemed pleased, or changing your opinion to fit the room are all ways of handing your happiness to someone else.

2.7.summary:
If outside events keep pulling you in different directions, make time to learn something worthwhile and stop spinning. But don't swing to the other extreme. Some people wear themselves out with constant activity yet have no real aim behind it, and they're just as much triflers as the easily distracted.

Busyness isn't the same as purpose. Everything you do should point towards some goal.
2.7.today: The person with back-to-back meetings and a full inbox who can't say what they're actually working towards is the modern example. So is filling every free minute with podcasts and tasks without asking what any of it is for.

2.8.summary: People rarely end up miserable because they failed to work out what someone else was thinking. They do end up miserable when they don't pay attention to what's going on in their own minds. Other people's thoughts are out of your hands; your own are the one thing you can actually examine and change.
2.8.today: Hours spent decoding a short text from a friend or guessing what a colleague meant by a comment would be better spent noticing your own mood, assumptions and reactions.

2.9.summary: Keep in mind what the universe is like, what you are like, and how you fit into it as a part of the whole. And remember that nobody can stop you from acting and speaking in a way that's true to your nature as a reasoning, social being. Circumstances can limit what you do, but not whether you do it well.

2.10.summary:
Theophrastus, the Greek philosopher who studied under Aristotle, argued that wrongs done out of desire are worse than wrongs done out of anger, and Marcus agrees. An angry person turns away from reason in pain, often in reaction to being hurt. Someone who does wrong for pleasure chooses it freely and enjoys it.

It's a striking reversal of what we might expect: the cool, comfortable self-indulgence can be worse than the hot outburst.
2.10.today: Snapping at a partner after a terrible day is wrong, but it's different from deliberately lying to them to enjoy something on the side. The first comes from pain; the second is a choice made for pleasure.

2.11.summary:
You could die at any moment, so let that shape what you do and think. Death isn't frightening: if there are gods, they won't harm you, and if there aren't, why want to live in a universe without them or without purpose? Marcus believes they exist and care, and have given us the power to avoid what is truly bad.

Death, life, fame, disgrace, pain and pleasure happen to good and bad people alike. Since they don't make anyone a better or worse person, they're not truly good or bad.

2.12.summary:
Everything vanishes fast, both things themselves and the memory of them. Your mind's job is to see through what pleasure lures you with, what pain frightens you with, and what fame dangles in front of you, and to recognise how flimsy and short-lived it all is. Ask who the people are whose opinions make up a reputation.

Look at death plainly too. Broken down into what it is, it's just a natural process, and fearing a natural process is childish.
2.12.today: The viral post nobody remembers a week later, the award that once seemed everything, the reviews you anxiously check: try asking whose opinions they really are and how long they'll last.

2.13.summary:
Few things are as wretched as running round in circles, poking into everything and trying to guess what's in other people's heads, when what you need is to look after your own inner sense of reason and conscience. Caring for it means keeping it free of strong emotion, carelessness and resentment.

What comes from the gods deserves respect. What comes from other people deserves affection, because they're family, and sometimes pity, because not knowing good from bad is a kind of blindness.
2.13.today: Scrolling through an acquaintance's posts trying to work out whether they're happy, or speculating about why a neighbour moved, is the circling Marcus means. Time spent on your own conduct pays off far better.

2.14.summary:
Even if you lived thousands of years, the only life you can lose is the one you're living now, because the present moment is all anyone actually has. You can't lose the past or the future, since you don't possess them. So a long life and a short one come to the same thing at the point of death.

Also, things repeat in cycles, so seeing them for a hundred years or two hundred makes little difference.

2.15.summary: Everything depends on how we see it. Monimus, a Cynic philosopher, said that all is opinion. Marcus thinks the saying is useful as long as you take the part of it that's true: it's our judgements about things, more than the things themselves, that make them seem good or bad.

2.16.summary:
There are five ways the soul harms itself. It becomes like a growth on the universe when it resents what happens. It turns away from people or sets out to hurt them in anger. It lets pleasure or pain overpower it. It pretends, saying or doing things it doesn't mean. And it acts without purpose, doing even small things thoughtlessly.

For Marcus, every action, however minor, should serve the goal of living by reason, as a citizen of the universe.
2.16.today: Fuming at the rain, giving a colleague the silent treatment, saying 'sounds great' when you mean the opposite, and an afternoon of aimless browsing are everyday versions of these five.

2.17.summary:
Life is brief and uncertain: the body decays, the mind whirls, luck is unpredictable and fame forgets. What can guide you through it? Only philosophy, which here means keeping your inner self steady: unharmed, above pleasure and pain, never aimless or false, not dependent on others, accepting whatever comes.

And it means waiting calmly for death, which is just the elements that make you breaking apart into new forms. Since that happens all the time in nature without harm, there's nothing to fear in it.
